newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin dismisses sauna-scandal justice minister.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin dismisses sauna-scandal justice minister.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin sacked Justice Minister Valentin Kovalyov on Wednesday in an apparent effort to end an unprecedented scandal over video film allegedly showing the minister in a gangland sauna with naked women.

The Kremlin said Yeltsin replaced the ex-communist Kovalyov, who had held his post since January 1995, with former security service chief Sergei Stepashin, who re-emerged after two years of disgace following a bloody Chechen raid in southern Russia.

Yeltsin suspended the justice minister just a week ago pending a probe into a newspaper report that he was filmed in a Moscow nightclub frequented by gangsters, relaxing in the steam room with several unidentified naked women in September 1995.
Television stations later screened excerpts of the tape.
Kovalyov, 53, suggested it was faked and had asked Yeltsin to suspend him to give him time to clear his name. But Interior Ministry officials said the grainy video was genuine.
"The most fascinating part of Kovalyov's story was not the pictures but rather the reaction to the newspaper revelations in top government circles," weekly magazine Itogi has said.
Moscow's elite has generally kept its private life hidden from the public and has made every effort not to allow scandals which periodically surfaced to interfere with high politics.

Other than a 1955 sex scandal in which several top Communists were sacked for visiting a secret brothel and the jailing of Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev's son-in-law for corruption, sleaze was almost never allowed to tarnish Soviet politics.
Despite widespread mistrust of politicians in post-Soviet Russia, where corruption is endemic, scandals are equally rare.

Media attention in the Kovalyov affair focused on the intrigues that may have been behind the release of the film rather than on the minister's behaviour. Many politicians reacted to the scandal with shows of solidarity for Kovalyov.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused the journalist of Sovershenno Sekretno (Top Secret) newspaper who wrote the story of breaking the law by encroaching on a minister's private life.
Ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky suggested the press could use the newspaper revelations to start a witch-hunt.
Prosecutor General Yuri Skuratov said the film alone gave no grounds for any kind of criminal investigation against Kovalyov.
"The bureaucrats stood up to defend one of their own," Itogi wrote in its Monday edition. "It is likely that Kovalyov will be quietly removed without any reference to the scandal."

Yeltsin appears to have at least partially broken the rule of silence by sacking the minister publicly while the scandal is still hot news. The Kremlin said his decree contained no detailed explanation as to why Kovalyov had been sacked.

But it said Yeltsin made the decision at the request of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who earlier asked him to sack Kovalyov. It is not clear whether the sacking meant the investigation launched last week was formally over.
"One has to admit that the president's decision is bold and quite unusual," one government official said.
"It is difficult to say how far Yeltsin may go in applying it to other similar situations but it certainly sets precedent of stronger public concern."
Kulikov, however, said Yeltsin had known of the film, seized during a probe into a banker charged with theft, as early as April, more than a month before the scandal broke in public.

For Stepashin, a former head of the Federal Security Service (FSB) the successor to the Soviet KGB, it was a return to prominence after a spell behind the scenes as head of the government's administrative department since November 1995.

Yeltsin sacked Stepashin, 45, from the FSB in June 1995 for mishandling a hostage-taking crisis in the southern Russian town of Budennovsk. At least 120 people were killed in the stand-off with Chechen separatist fighters who subsequently escaped.
